title: One-Hot Encoding Visualizer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: See what pd.get_dummies returns for a categorical column, switch drop_first and dtype, add a new category, and trace each row to the column that marks it.

learningObjectives: Students will be able to explain how one-hot encoding turns a categorical column into True/False columns, predict the columns `pd.get_dummies` creates with and without `drop_first=True`, and explain why dropping one column avoids the dummy variable trap.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Before-and-after tables with switches for the encoder's options and row-by-row tracing
keyQuestions: Why does every row sum to 1 when all the columns are kept?
How can you tell which category a row belongs to when it is False in every column?
What decides which category pandas drops, and how could that surprise you?
commonMisconceptions: Categories can simply be replaced by the numbers 1, 2, 3 (that invents an order and equal spacing that the categories do not have).
drop_first=True throws away the information about one category (that category is still identified by the rows that are False in every remaining column).
pandas drops the last category, or the least common one (it drops the first label in sorted order).
get_dummies returns 1s and 0s (current pandas returns True and False unless dtype=int is passed; both behave the same way in arithmetic).
assessmentOpportunities: Given a column `size` with the values Small, Medium, Large, Medium, students write the column names and the first two rows returned by `pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['size'], drop_first=True)`, name the reference category, and explain why it is Large and not Small.
